notes: Food for home consumption is exempt, but candy and soft drinks are taxed at the full 6.625%, which is not counted here (both are exempt when bought with SNAP benefits).
Alcohol is taxed at 6.625%, packaged or by the drink. In Atlantic City, drinks served also carry the 3% luxury tax (9.625% in all), counted for drinks served there (local rates table).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 6.625%, on top of excise taxes ($3.00 a pack, 30 cents a milliliter of liquid nicotine and 30% of the retail price of container e-liquid since August 1, 2025).
Household supplies: diapers (children's and adult), baby wipes and disposable paper products for household use are exempt, which is not taken out here; detergents and cleaners are taxed.
Personal care products: menstrual products and over-the-counter drugs are exempt, which is not taken out here; soap, shampoo, toothpaste and cosmetics are taxed.

Barber and beauty services are not taxed, but massage (unless prescribed), tanning and tattooing are, which is not counted here; health and fitness club memberships are taxed too (not shown, since fitness has no tax figures).

Clothing and footwear are exempt; fur clothing, accessories and sport equipment are taxed, which is not counted here. The yearly back-to-school sales tax holiday was repealed in 2024 (P.L. 2024, c. 19); a 2026 bill to restore one has not passed.
Laundry and dry cleaning: laundering and dry cleaning of clothing are not taxed; cleaning of other items is.

Motor fuel is exempt from sales tax. The per-gallon taxes, left out here, come to 49.1 cents for gasoline (10.5-cent motor fuels tax and 38.6-cent petroleum products gross receipts tax) since January 1, 2026; the rate is reset each January 1, and the 2027 rate is not yet announced. No 2026 gas tax holiday was enacted.
Repair labor and parts are taxed; a $1.50 fee applies to each new tire.

In Urban Enterprise Zones (32 zones in 37 municipalities, designated through June 30, 2032) and in Salem County, certified sellers charge half the rate (3.3125%) on goods sold in person at their location there, but not on prepared food, alcohol, cigarettes, motor vehicles, energy or services. It is not counted here, since only certified sellers charge it; the zones' and county's pages say so.

Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus a 5% State Occupancy Fee and, in 214 municipalities, a municipal occupancy tax of up to 3% (8 more tax only short-term rentals; Division of Taxation list of October 5, 2026). Atlantic City, Newark, Jersey City and Elizabeth pay a 1% state fee instead, Newark and Jersey City add 6% city hotel taxes, Atlantic City its 9% luxury tax (with the sales tax cut to 3.625%) and per-room fees, and the Wildwoods a 3.15% state fee, the 2% tourism sales tax and a 1.85% assessment. None of the hotel taxes is counted here.

The 2% Cape May County tourism sales tax on restaurant food and drink in Wildwood, North Wildwood and Wildwood Crest is counted in their restaurant rate (local rates table); Atlantic City's luxury tax does not apply to food.
gaps: New Jersey has no local general sales tax; the 6.625% state rate applies almost everywhere.

programs: No statewide map of New Jersey's special improvement districts exists (the state's last census of them dates from 2010-11). Mapped here: Newark's (the city's 2021 map), Middlesex County's (New Brunswick, Woodbridge, Highland Park, Metuchen, Carteret and Perth Amboy) and the Main Street districts, many of which are also improvement districts. Not mapped (no official map found): Jersey City's (Historic Downtown, Journal Square, Central Avenue, McGinley Square, Exchange Place and West Side Avenue: the city publishes no layer of them, and a volunteer group's layer isn't an official map; its Jackson Hill Main Street district is shown as a Main Street district), Paterson's, Elizabeth's (Elizabeth Avenue and Historic Midtown), Trenton's, Camden's and Atlantic City's.

Areas in need of redevelopment come from the Department of Community Affairs' statewide map (365 municipalities), which is incomplete for declarations made before July 2003. Transit Villages aren't shown: they have no legal boundaries. The Department of State's Office for Planning Advocacy publishes the 35 designated stations as points with half-mile planning buffers, which it says are not legal boundaries (edited October 2024).

New Jersey's 2026 Municipal Revitalization Index (Department of Community Affairs) ranks the state's 564 municipalities by distress, 1 the most distressed; the pages of the places scoring 50 or more of 100 give their rank. Townships scoring 50 or more, which the site doesn't list as places: Commercial (Cumberland County, rank 21), Fairfield (Cumberland County, rank 23), City of Orange (Essex County, rank 24), Maurice River (Cumberland County, rank 26), Irvington (Essex County, rank 32) and New Hanover (Burlington County, rank 36).

Newark's special improvement districts are mapped as the city drew them in April 2021, from the state's 2018 census of districts; several have been amended since, so their current boundaries may differ. The Greater Newark Tourism Improvement District, an assessment on hotels, isn't shown.

Newark ranks 18 of 564 on New Jersey's 2026 Municipal Revitalization Index (1 is the most distressed; distress score 62.5 of 100), which the state uses to target aid and programs (Department of Community Affairs).

Jersey City's special improvement districts (Historic Downtown, Journal Square, Central Avenue, McGinley Square, Exchange Place and West Side Avenue) aren't mapped: the city publishes no layer of them (its open data has only a 2018 point list of West Side Avenue businesses), and a volunteer group's layer (Sustainable Jersey City, 2026) isn't an official map. The Jackson Hill Main Street special improvement district (created in 2012) is shown as a Main Street district.

Paterson's special improvement districts aren't mapped (no official map found), and the state's map of areas in need of redevelopment shows none in Paterson, though the city has declared some; its record there is likely incomplete.

Paterson ranks 11 of 564 on New Jersey's 2026 Municipal Revitalization Index (1 is the most distressed; distress score 71.1 of 100), which the state uses to target aid and programs (Department of Community Affairs).
